questions.q: According to the lesson, what is usually behind an agent's failures?
options: The model isn't capable enough, so the first fix is a larger model
The agent has too few tools, so it can't reach the data it needs
The brief is written too calmly, so the model ignores important rules
Vague tools, missing instructions or no clear point at which to stop
questions.explain: The lesson says the model is rarely the culprit; failures usually come from vague tools, missing instructions or no clear stopping point, which is why it gives templates for all three.

questions.q: Your agent's step log shows it calling the same tool again and again with the same input. What does the lesson point to as the likely cause?
options: The tool's name is too short, so the agent can't tell what it does
The tool returns unhelpful errors, so the agent doesn't know what to try next
The tool returns too few fields, so it should send the full raw record instead
The brief lacks capital-letter warnings, so the agent ignores its step limit
questions.explain: When you test, loops where the agent repeats the same call usually signal unhelpful errors; a good error message tells the agent what to try next.

questions.q: You're writing the brief for an order-support agent. Which rule best follows the lesson's advice?
options: NEVER GUESS TRACKING NUMBERS. THIS IS CRITICAL. DO NOT EVER GUESS.
Handle every customer request yourself and avoid escalating whenever possible.
Never guess tracking numbers, because customers act on them.
Use whatever tools seem useful, and decide for yourself when you're done.
questions.explain: The lesson recommends explaining the why behind important rules and skipping the shouting, because reasons generalize better and capital-letter warnings can make models overly cautious.
